title: Moore pushed to do more for community on Transgender Day of Visibility
summary: What started as a day to recognize the state’s transgender community spun into pointed criticism of the Moore administration's and state lawmakers' failure to protect transgender individuals, and spilled into a back-and-forth on the House floor Monday.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters March 31, 2025

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters March 31, 2025

What started as a day to recognize the state’s transgender community spun into pointed criticism of the Moore administration’s and state lawmakers’ failure to protect against Trump administration actions that affect the day-to-day lives of transgender individuals.

The topic of transgender issues later spilled out into a debate on the House floor, reflecting a tumultuous time for transgender people even in the so-called “safe haven” that is Maryland.

The tension began Monday morning at an International Transgender Day of Visibility event hosted by Gov. Wes Moore (D) in the State House. During his remarks, he promised that transgender Marylanders will continue to be protected in the state even as President Donald Trump (R) signals hostility towards the community.

“We are proud to be a safe haven for people of all backgrounds and identities, and I want to be very clear, this is a reputation that we intend on keeping,” he said, highlighting policies in recent years that help support LGBTQ+ veterans and grant better access to gender-affirming care.

But to Lee Blinder — a nonbinary official who chairs the Maryland Commission on LGBTQIA+ Affairs in the Governor’s Office — those promises have fallen flat.

“We know who you, Governor Moore, can be for us,” Blinder said as Moore stood nearby, “and I am here begging you to do it.

“It will not get easier to support trans people. It will not get easier to commit to this community, it will only get harder in the days that come,” Blinder said.

Blinder criticized what they called the administration’s lack of support to protect the community amid federal measures to diminish the presence of transgender people in day-to-day life.

Blinder noted that bills impacting the LGBTQ+ community are not moving this session — including Senate Bill 314, the Birth Certificate Modernization Act, which would make it easier for transgender people to make changes to their birth certificates, among other measures.

They also said more state dollars should be going towards the transgender community, even as lawmakers discuss billions in cuts to state programs and more than $1 billion in new revenue increases to address a fiscal 2026 budget shortfall.

“We’re facing one of the most dangerous threats to trans lives across the country, and the trans community is nowhere to be found in here with this budget, so now I must beg,” Blinder said. “I’ll beg in private; I’ll beg in public. I’ll do absolutely whatever it takes to get my community what we need.”

Moore did not directly respond to the criticism at the event and did not take questions from press. He wrapped up by declaring March 31 Transgender Day of Visibility in the state, as he has done each year during his term.

The governor’s office later reiterated Moore’s commitment to be a safe haven for the transgender community, pointing to policies that include increased funding for hate crime prevention in fiscal 2026 and providing Medicaid access to gender-affirming health care resources.

“We are proud of our work so far, but our administration knows we have so much more to do — and we will do it together in partnership,” the statement said.

Following the morning event, Blinder said that the governor’s compassion for the transgender community is “not in question.” But Blinder felt a duty to speak up.

“This is a desperate time, and we are in a state of emergency,” they said. “This community is in crisis, and they are relying on me. So, I have to do a difficult thing and share an honest report with the governor, we really deserve and need that protection.”

The fight over transgender issues continued onto the House floor later Monday.

Del. Kathy Szeliga (R-Baltimore County) stood to recognize National Woman’s History Month by speaking in support of Riley Gaines, a former University of Kentucky swimmer who tied with transgender University of Pennsylvania swimmer Lia Thomas in the NCAA championship in 2022.

Gaines’ experience is cited by those pushing for policies that ban transgender women from women’s sports, arguing that they have inherent strengths and unfair advantages against cisgender women.

“Women accomplish in sports and they stand on their own. As women, we are competitive and resilient and determined. We were created with unique strengths, very different from men, and we should never be able to blur those truths,” Szeliga said to applause and whistles of approval. “Riley Gaines has inspired many other girls and women to speak up. She has faced threats, violence and hatred … but she keeps showing up for girls in sports.”

International Transgender Day of Visibility always falls on March 31, which also happens to be the last day of National Women’s History Month. Del. Kris Fair (D-Frederick) shot back against Szeliga’s “unfortunate” comments and brought the conversation back to Transgender Day of Visibility.

“It’s a day to celebrate the lives and contributions that trans people bring to every single region of this country, every single region to this state,” he said. “Trans women are women — they deserve the same respect, kindness and compassion as every other woman in this country.”

He said transgender individuals “are veterans, they are hardworking employees, they are people who contribute to our society, they sit on the boards of our non-profits, they work in our schools, they help our families, and they support their own families. And they have to suffer through the indignity of having to sit here and be erased on this floor. I will not stand for it.”

“I say to all the trans people out there in Maryland listening to us right now — Happy Trans Day of Visibility. We love you, we see you, we affirm you,” Fair concluded, as many of the Democratic members stood to applaud.

After the floor session, Fair said he wanted to “correct the record” and affirm “that trans people are very important to our society.”

“Unfortunately, one of my colleagues felt it necessary to use today as a political football, and then trash transgender people, disrespect them on the floor,” he said.

As to Blinder’s comments, Fair agreed that the House is struggling to pass some of the LGBTQ+ bills this session, but he said Maryland is still “light years ahead of other states” in supporting transgender and the LGBTQ+ population.

“I hear the chair’s comments. And I agree we can always be doing more, always … Maryland is at the upper echelon of protections for transgender people and for LGBTQ+ people,” he said, “but that never means that we’ve done enough, there’s more to do.”
